name: Bits → bytes
description: Converts a number of bits to bytes by dividing by 8, since one byte contains eight bits. It expresses data volume in the larger byte unit.
notes: This is the standard 8 bits per byte. Note that storage sizes use bytes while transmission rates are often quoted in bits, so the two differ by a factor of 8.

name: Gibibytes → bytes
description: Converts gibibytes to bytes by multiplying by 1024 cubed (1,073,741,824). Gibibytes are the binary-based unit, distinct from decimal gigabytes.
notes: A gibibyte (GiB) uses 1024³ bytes, while a gigabyte (GB) is 1000³ bytes; the two differ by about 7%. Use this for binary GiB, not decimal GB.

name: Mbps → MB/s
description: Converts a bit rate in megabits per second to megabytes per second by dividing by 8. It shows how fast data transfers in byte terms from a bit-based speed.
notes: Divides by 8 bits per byte; this mixes decimal-megabit rates with megabytes, so it is the common networking convention rather than binary MiB. A 100 Mbps link is about 12.5 MB/s.

name: File transfer time
description: Estimates the time to transfer a file as its size in megabytes times 8, divided by the link speed in megabits per second. The factor of 8 converts bytes to bits so units match.
notes: Size is in megabytes and speed in megabits per second, giving seconds. This is an ideal estimate that ignores protocol overhead, latency, and real-world throughput loss.

name: Bit rate
description: Computes the bit rate as the amount of data in bits divided by the transfer duration, giving bits per second. It measures how quickly data flows over time.
notes: Data size must be in bits and duration in seconds to get bits per second. If your data is in bytes, multiply by 8 first.

name: Shannon channel capacity
description: Computes the Shannon-Hartley maximum error-free data rate of a channel as bandwidth times the base-2 logarithm of one plus the signal-to-noise ratio. It sets the theoretical upper limit on reliable throughput.
notes: SNR is entered as a linear power ratio, not in decibels. Bandwidth is in hertz and the result in bits per second is a theoretical ceiling, unreachable in practice.

name: Nyquist Sampling Rate
description: Gives the minimum sampling rate for a signal as twice its maximum frequency, the Nyquist rate. Sampling at or above this rate lets the original signal be reconstructed without aliasing.
notes: This is a theoretical minimum; real systems sample somewhat higher and add an anti-aliasing filter. The signal must be band-limited to fmax for the rule to hold.

name: Nyquist Maximum Data Rate
description: Gives the maximum data rate of a noiseless channel as 2×B×log2(M), from bandwidth B and the number of discrete signal levels M. More levels or wider bandwidth carry more bits per second.
notes: Applies to an ideal noiseless channel; with noise, use the Shannon capacity instead. M is the number of signal levels, so each symbol carries log2(M) bits.

name: Channel Capacity (SNR ratio)
description: The Shannon–Hartley theorem gives the maximum error-free capacity of a noisy channel as B×log2(1+SNR), from bandwidth B and the signal-to-noise ratio. It is the upper limit on reliable data rate.
notes: SNR is a linear power ratio here, not decibels; convert dB with 10^(dB/10) first. This is a theoretical ceiling that real coding schemes only approach.

name: Bandwidth-Delay Product
description: Gives the bandwidth-delay product as bandwidth times round-trip time, the number of bits in transit on the link at once. It sets the buffer or window size needed to keep a link fully utilised.
notes: Bandwidth in bits per second and RTT in seconds give the result in bits; divide by 8 for bytes. A TCP window smaller than this value limits throughput below the link's capacity.

name: Usable Hosts per Subnet
description: Gives the number of usable host addresses in a subnet as 2^h − 2, from the number of host bits h. The subtraction removes the reserved network and broadcast addresses.
notes: The −2 accounts for the network and broadcast addresses; with 0 or 1 host bits the classic formula yields none. IPv6 and some point-to-point cases do not reserve these two.

name: Number of Subnets
description: Gives the number of equal-size subnets created when you borrow n bits from the host portion of an address. Each borrowed bit doubles the count, so the total is 2 raised to the power n.
notes: n is the number of subnet bits borrowed, not the prefix length. Some older schemes reserve the all-zeros and all-ones subnets, reducing the usable count.

name: IPv4 Addresses in Prefix
description: Counts the total IPv4 addresses contained in a block with the given prefix length p. Since IPv4 has 32 bits, the host portion is 32 minus p bits, giving 2 to the power of that as the address count.
notes: This is the raw total; in a normal subnet the network and broadcast addresses are not assignable to hosts, so usable hosts are two fewer (except for /31 and /32).

name: Throughput
description: Computes the average data transfer rate by dividing the amount of data moved by the time it took. The result is expressed in bits per second.
notes: Keep data in bits and time in seconds for bps; if data is in bytes, multiply by 8 first. This is an average rate, not the instantaneous peak.

name: Propagation Delay
description: Gives the time a signal takes to travel a link, found by dividing the link distance by the propagation speed of the signal in the medium. The result is in seconds.
notes: This is only propagation delay, not transmission, queuing, or processing delay. Propagation speed in cables is typically 0.6 to 0.7 times the speed of light in vacuum.

name: Audio Bit Rate (PCM)
description: Calculates the raw bit rate of uncompressed PCM audio by multiplying the sample rate, the bit depth per sample, and the number of channels. The result is in bits per second.
notes: This applies to uncompressed PCM only; compressed formats like MP3 or AAC use far lower rates. Multiply by duration to estimate file size in bits.

name: Uncompressed Video Bit Rate
description: Estimates the bit rate of raw uncompressed video by multiplying the frame width and height in pixels by the frame rate and the color depth per pixel. The result is in bits per second.
notes: This is the uncompressed rate; real codecs such as H.264 or H.265 reduce it by orders of magnitude. Color depth here is total bits per pixel across all channels.

name: File Size from Bit Rate
description: Gives the size of a media file by multiplying its bit rate by its duration. With bit rate in bits per second and duration in seconds, the result is the total size in bits.
notes: Divide by 8 for bytes, and by 8 million for megabytes. This assumes a constant bit rate; variable-bit-rate streams give only an approximate size.

name: Compression Ratio
description: Expresses how much a file was compressed as the ratio of the original size to the compressed size. A value of 4 means the original is four times larger than the compressed version.
notes: Both sizes must use the same unit. This is a ratio, not a percentage; for the fraction of space saved use a separate space-saving formula.

name: Space Saving
description: Gives the fraction of storage saved by compression, computed as one minus the compressed size divided by the original size. A result of 0.75 means 75 percent of the space was saved.
notes: Result is a fraction from 0 to 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Both sizes must share the same unit, and the compressed size should not exceed the original.

name: RAID 5 Usable Capacity
description: Gives the usable storage of a RAID 5 array as the number of drives minus one, multiplied by the capacity of a single drive. One drive's worth of space is consumed by distributed parity.
notes: Assumes all drives are the same size; a mixed array is limited by the smallest drive. RAID 5 tolerates the failure of one drive only.

name: RAID 6 Usable Capacity
description: Gives the usable storage of a RAID 6 array as the number of drives minus two, multiplied by the capacity of a single drive. Two drives' worth of space is used for dual parity.
notes: Assumes uniform drive sizes; a mixed array is capped by the smallest drive. RAID 6 tolerates the simultaneous failure of any two drives.

name: RAID 10 Usable Capacity
description: Gives the usable storage of a RAID 10 array as half the number of drives multiplied by the capacity of a single drive, since every drive is mirrored by a partner.
notes: Requires an even number of same-size drives. It survives multiple drive failures only if no complete mirror pair is lost at once.

name: Error-Correction Capability
description: Gives how many bit errors a block code can correct, as the floor of the minimum Hamming distance minus one, divided by two. A code with minimum distance 5 can correct up to two errors.
notes: dmin is the minimum Hamming distance between valid codewords. The result is a whole number of correctable errors; detection capability is higher than correction.

name: Hash Table Load Factor
description: Gives a hash table's load factor as the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. It measures how full the table is and predicts collision likelihood.
notes: For open addressing the load factor stays at or below 1; for chaining it can exceed 1. Higher load factors slow lookups, so tables are often resized near a threshold.

name: Exponential Complexity O(2^n)
description: Gives the number of basic operations for an algorithm with exponential time complexity of order 2 to the n, where n is the input size. The count doubles with each additional unit of input.
notes: This is an asymptotic order-of-growth estimate, not an exact operation count. Even modest n values become computationally infeasible very quickly.

name: Cache Hit Ratio
description: Gives the fraction of memory accesses served from cache, as the number of hits divided by the total of hits plus misses. A value near 1 means the cache is very effective.
notes: Hits and misses must be counts over the same period. The hit ratio and miss ratio always sum to 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Cache Miss Ratio
description: Gives the fraction of memory accesses not found in cache, as the number of misses divided by the total of hits plus misses. A lower value indicates better cache performance.
notes: Counts must cover the same interval. The miss ratio equals one minus the hit ratio; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Cycles Per Instruction (CPI)
description: Gives the average number of clock cycles a processor spends per instruction, as total clock cycles divided by total instructions executed. Lower CPI means higher efficiency per instruction.
notes: This is an average over a workload; individual instructions vary widely in cycle cost. CPI is the reciprocal of instructions per cycle (IPC).

name: MIPS Rate
description: Gives a processor's rate in millions of instructions per second, as the clock frequency divided by the cycles per instruction and by one million. It combines clock speed and efficiency into a throughput figure.
notes: Enter frequency in hertz. MIPS depends on the instruction mix, so it is unreliable for comparing different instruction-set architectures.

name: Amdahl's Speedup
description: Gives the overall speedup from parallelizing a program, where p is the parallelizable fraction sped up by a factor s. The serial part 1 minus p limits the achievable gain.
notes: Enter p as a fraction from 0 to 1. Speedup is capped by the serial portion, so improving s eventually yields diminishing returns.

name: Amdahl Maximum Speedup
description: Gives the theoretical upper limit on speedup under Amdahl's law when the parallel part is infinitely fast, as one divided by the serial fraction 1 minus p. This is the ceiling no amount of parallelism can exceed.
notes: Enter p as a fraction; only the serial fraction matters here. For example a 90 percent parallel program can never exceed a 10x speedup.

name: Gustafson Scaled Speedup
description: Gives the scaled speedup under Gustafson's law for n processors when the serial fraction is s, as n minus n minus one times s. It models keeping run time fixed while enlarging the problem.
notes: Enter s as a fraction of the work that stays serial. Unlike Amdahl's law it assumes the workload grows with the processor count, so speedup scales more optimistically.

name: Clock Period
description: Gives the duration of one clock cycle as the reciprocal of the clock frequency. A 3 GHz clock, for instance, has a period of about 0.33 nanoseconds.
notes: Enter frequency in hertz to get the period in seconds. The clock period is the inverse of frequency, so faster clocks have shorter periods.

name: Memory Address Space
description: Gives the number of distinct addresses an address bus can reference, as 2 raised to the width of the bus in bits. A 32-bit bus can address about 4.29 billion locations.
notes: This counts addressable units, usually bytes, not total capacity in bits. A 32-bit address space corresponds to 4 GiB when each address is one byte.

name: Two-Digit Hex to Decimal
description: Converts a two-digit hexadecimal number to decimal by multiplying the high digit's value by 16 and adding the low digit's value. For example FF gives 255.
notes: Each digit value must be between 0 and 15, where A through F correspond to 10 through 15. The result ranges from 0 to 255, matching one byte.

name: Goodput (with loss)
description: Gives the effective useful throughput, or goodput, as the raw bandwidth multiplied by the fraction of data that is not lost, that is one minus the loss fraction. It reflects data actually delivered.
notes: Enter loss as a fraction from 0 to 1, not a percentage. This simple model accounts only for loss, not protocol overhead or retransmission timing.

name: Bit Error Rate (BER)
description: Gives the bit error rate as the number of bits received in error divided by the total number of bits transmitted. It measures the reliability of a digital transmission link.
notes: Both counts must be over the same transmission. BER is a dimensionless ratio, often extremely small and written in scientific notation such as 5e-6.

name: Packets Needed
description: Gives the number of packets required to carry a payload, as the total payload size divided by the payload capacity per packet, rounded up. Any leftover data needs one more full packet.
notes: The ceiling accounts for a final partial packet. mtu here is usable payload per packet, not the full frame including headers, so use the correct value.

name: CPU Execution Time
description: Gives the time a CPU takes to run a program, as the instruction count multiplied by the cycles per instruction and divided by the clock frequency. It links the three classic performance factors.
notes: Enter frequency in hertz to get time in seconds. This is the CPU time only, excluding waiting on I/O or memory stalls beyond what CPI captures.

name: Effective Memory Access Time
description: Gives the average memory access time as a weighted blend of cache and main-memory times: the hit rate times the cache access time plus the miss rate times the memory access time. Misses dominate the average unless the hit rate is very high.
notes: Enter the hit rate as a fraction from 0 to 1; the miss rate is one minus it. A simple two-level model that ignores miss penalties like page faults.

name: Symbol Rate (Baud)
description: Gives the symbol rate in baud as the bit rate divided by the number of bits carried per symbol. When each symbol carries more than one bit, the baud rate is lower than the bit rate.
notes: Baud counts symbols per second, not bits per second; the two are equal only when each symbol carries one bit. Higher-order modulation packs more bits per symbol.

name: Frame Period
description: Gives the time between successive frames as the reciprocal of the frame rate. At 60 frames per second, for example, each frame lasts about 16.7 milliseconds.
notes: Enter the frame rate in frames per second to get the period in seconds. The frame period is the inverse of frame rate, so higher rates give shorter frame times.

name: Little's Law (Items in System)
description: Gives the average number of items in a stable system as the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. It holds regardless of the arrival or service distribution.
notes: The rates and times must use consistent units, and the system must be in steady state. It counts items being served plus those waiting.

name: Server Utilization
description: Gives a single server's utilization, or traffic intensity, as the arrival rate divided by the service rate. A value of 0.8 means the server is busy 80 percent of the time.
notes: Arrival and service rates must use the same time unit. For a stable single-server queue this ratio must stay below 1, or the queue grows without bound.

name: M/M/1 Average Number in System
description: Gives the average number of customers in an M/M/1 queue as the traffic intensity rho divided by one minus rho. As rho approaches 1, the average number grows without bound.
notes: Valid only for a stable queue where rho is below 1. It assumes Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, and a single server.

name: Disk Capacity (CHS)
description: Gives a disk's raw capacity in bytes from its cylinder-head-sector geometry, by multiplying the number of cylinders, heads, sectors per track, and bytes per sector together.
notes: This gives raw geometric capacity; usable space is less after formatting. Modern drives use logical block addressing, so reported CHS values are often virtual rather than physical.

name: Nibbles in Data
description: Gives the number of nibbles in a block of data by dividing the number of bits by four, since one nibble is four bits. A nibble corresponds to a single hexadecimal digit.
notes: The bit count should be a multiple of 4 for a whole number of nibbles. Two nibbles make one byte, so the nibble count is twice the byte count.

name: Moore's Law (Transistor Count)
description: Projects transistor count over time using Moore's Law, N0*2^(t/T), where N0 is the starting count, t the elapsed years, and T the doubling period. It models the historical exponential growth of chip transistor density.
notes: The classic doubling period is about 2 years, though some formulations use 18 months or other values. t and T must use the same time unit.

name: RAID 0 Usable Capacity
description: Computes the usable storage capacity of a RAID 0 (striped) array, n*d, where n is the number of disks and d the capacity of each. Striping combines all disk capacity with no redundancy overhead.
notes: All disks are assumed to have equal capacity d; a RAID 0 array offers no fault tolerance, so any single disk failure loses all data. The result uses the same capacity unit as d.

name: Minimum Bits to Represent N Values
description: Gives the minimum number of bits needed to represent N distinct values, ceil(log2(N)). This is the standard binary encoding lower bound used in data structures and information theory.
notes: N must be a positive integer greater than or equal to 1. For example, N=256 requires 8 bits, since 2^8 = 256 exactly.

name: Serialization (Transmission) Delay
description: Computes the time needed to push all bits of a packet onto a link as the packet size in bits divided by the link rate in bits per second. It is the delay from clocking the frame out, separate from how far the signal travels.
notes: Packet size must be in bits, so convert from bytes by multiplying by 8. This transmission delay does not include propagation, queuing, or processing delay.

name: Cable Propagation Delay
description: Computes how long a signal takes to travel a given distance through a cable whose velocity factor scales the speed of light. It divides distance by the actual propagation speed, the velocity factor times 3×10⁸ m/s.
notes: The velocity factor is a fraction between 0 and 1, typically around 0.6 to 0.7 for copper and fiber. This is one-way delay and depends only on distance, not on data rate.

name: Round-Trip Propagation Time
description: Computes the round-trip propagation time as twice the one-way distance divided by the propagation speed. It is the time for a signal to reach the far end and return, ignoring transmission and processing.
notes: Enter the one-way distance; the factor of 2 accounts for the return path. This is propagation only, so real round-trip time also includes serialization, queuing, and processing delays.

name: Bulk Data Download Time
description: Estimates the time to download a file by converting its size in bytes to bits and dividing by the throughput in bits per second. It gives the ideal transfer time assuming the throughput is sustained.
notes: File size is in bytes and is multiplied by 8 to match the bit-based rate. Real downloads take longer because of protocol overhead, congestion, and connection setup.

name: Data Transferred (Bytes)
description: Computes how many bytes are transferred over a duration at a constant bit rate, multiplying rate by time and dividing by 8 to convert bits to bytes. It answers how much data moves during the interval.
notes: The bit rate is in bits per second and the result is in bytes, hence the division by 8. This assumes a steady rate over the whole duration with no idle gaps.

name: TCP Throughput (Window/RTT)
description: Estimates the maximum TCP throughput as the window size delivered once per round-trip time. It converts the window from bytes to bits and divides by the RTT, giving the ceiling imposed by the window when there is no loss.
notes: Window size is in bytes and multiplied by 8; RTT is in seconds. Reaching this rate needs a window at least equal to the bandwidth-delay product, and actual throughput can be lower under loss.

name: TCP Optimal Window Size
description: Computes the bandwidth-delay product, the ideal TCP window in bytes to keep a link fully utilized. It multiplies bandwidth by round-trip time and divides by 8 to convert the bit-based result into bytes.
notes: Bandwidth is in bits per second and RTT in seconds; the division by 8 gives bytes. A window smaller than this underuses the link, so high-latency high-speed paths need window scaling.

name: Mathis Equation (TCP Throughput)
description: Estimates long-term TCP throughput under random loss using the Mathis model. Throughput scales with the segment size and inversely with the round-trip time and the square root of the packet loss probability.
notes: Segment size is in bytes and multiplied by 8; loss probability is a fraction, not a percent. The model assumes small, independent losses and breaks down as loss approaches zero, giving unbounded rates.

name: Throughput with Packet Loss
description: Computes the effective throughput after a fraction of packets is lost, scaling the raw rate by one minus the loss fraction. It gives the portion of the line rate that reaches the receiver as useful data.
notes: The loss fraction is a value between 0 and 1, not a percentage. This is a simple linear model and does not capture the sharper throughput collapse that TCP suffers under loss.

name: Goodput (Protocol Overhead)
description: Computes goodput, the useful application throughput, by scaling the line rate by the ratio of payload bytes to total frame bytes. Header bytes consume link capacity without carrying application data, so goodput is always below the line rate.
notes: Payload and header are both in bytes; the line rate must exceed the goodput. This counts one header per payload and ignores retransmissions and inter-frame gaps.

name: Frame Efficiency (Payload Ratio)
description: Computes frame efficiency as the fraction of each frame that is payload, dividing payload bytes by the sum of payload and overhead bytes. A value near 1 means little overhead relative to the data carried.
notes: Payload and overhead must be in the same byte units. Overhead should include all framing, headers, and trailers per frame; larger payloads raise efficiency toward 1.

name: Bit Rate from Baud (M-ary)
description: Computes the bit rate from the symbol rate for M-ary modulation, multiplying the baud rate by the number of bits each symbol carries, which is log2 of the number of levels. More levels pack more bits into every symbol.
notes: M is the number of distinct symbols, so M must be a power of 2 for an integer bit count. Bandwidth still limits the baud rate, and higher M needs a better signal-to-noise ratio.

name: Coded Data Rate (FEC)
description: Computes the useful information rate after forward error correction, scaling the channel rate by the code rate k over n. The parity bits added for error correction reduce the throughput available for actual data.
notes: Here k is information bits and n the total coded bits per block, so k must be less than n. This gives only the raw information rate and does not account for coding gain or residual errors.

name: Subnet Address Count (IPv4)
description: Computes the total number of IPv4 addresses in a subnet as 2 raised to the number of host bits, which is 32 minus the prefix length. A shorter prefix leaves more host bits and thus more addresses.
notes: This is the raw address count; usable hosts are normally two fewer for the network and broadcast addresses. The prefix length must be between 0 and 32.

name: M/M/1 Mean Time in System
description: Computes the mean time a customer spends in an M/M/1 queue, including waiting and service, as one over the difference between the service rate and the arrival rate. Delay grows sharply as arrivals approach the service capacity.
notes: The service rate must exceed the arrival rate or the queue is unstable and the formula is invalid. Both rates use the same time unit, and this is total time in system, not just waiting time.

name: M/M/1 Mean Number in System
description: Computes the mean number of customers in an M/M/1 system, both waiting and in service, as the utilization divided by one minus the utilization. The count rises steeply as utilization nears 1.
notes: Utilization rho is the arrival rate over the service rate and must be below 1 for stability. As rho approaches 1 the mean number grows without bound.

name: Little's Law (Response Time)
description: Applies Little's Law to find the average time an item spends in a system as the average number in the system divided by the arrival rate. It links how full a system is to how long items linger there.
notes: The items count and arrival rate must be measured over the same steady-state period. Little's Law holds for any stable system regardless of its internal service discipline.

name: Traffic Intensity (Erlangs)
description: Computes offered traffic in erlangs as the call arrival rate times the mean holding time per call. One erlang represents one circuit continuously occupied, so the result estimates how many channels are busy on average.
notes: Arrival rate and holding time must use consistent time units so the product is dimensionless. Erlangs measure offered load and can exceed the number of available circuits, causing blocking.

name: Slotted ALOHA Throughput
description: Computes the throughput of slotted ALOHA as the offered load G times e to the power of minus G. The result is the fraction of slots carrying a successful transmission, peaking at about 0.368 when G equals 1.
notes: G is the mean number of transmission attempts per slot, including retransmissions. Throughput falls off on both sides of G equal to 1, so overload actually reduces useful traffic.

name: Pure ALOHA Throughput
description: Computes the throughput of pure ALOHA as the offered load G times e to the power of minus 2G. Because frames can collide over a doubled vulnerable window, it peaks at only about 0.184 when G equals 0.5.
notes: G is the mean transmission attempts per frame time, including retransmissions. Pure ALOHA achieves half the peak throughput of slotted ALOHA due to its wider collision window.

name: Stop-and-Wait ARQ Efficiency
description: Computes the link efficiency of stop-and-wait ARQ as one over one plus twice the ratio a of propagation to transmission time. It shows how idle waiting for each acknowledgment lowers utilization.
notes: The parameter a is the propagation delay divided by the frame transmission time, assuming error-free transfer. Large a, as on long or fast links, makes stop-and-wait very inefficient.

name: Sliding Window Efficiency
description: Computes the efficiency of a sliding-window protocol as the window size divided by one plus twice the propagation-to-transmission ratio a, capped at 1. A large enough window keeps the link fully busy and reaches efficiency 1.
notes: The min with 1 caps efficiency once the window covers the full round-trip. The parameter a is propagation over transmission time, and error-free transfer is assumed.

name: RTP Interarrival Jitter
description: Updates the RTP interarrival jitter estimate by adding one sixteenth of the difference between the latest absolute delay variation and the previous jitter. This exponential filter smooths jitter as defined in RFC 3550.
notes: Delay variation d can be signed but its absolute value is used, and 1/16 is the fixed RFC 3550 gain. The estimate is in the same time units as the inputs and tracks changes gradually.

name: Smoothed RTT (EWMA)
description: Updates the smoothed round-trip time with an exponentially weighted moving average, blending the previous estimate and the new sample by the smoothing factor alpha. A larger alpha makes the estimate respond faster to recent samples.
notes: Alpha lies between 0 and 1; TCP commonly uses 1/8. The smoothed RTT and sample share the same time units, and this update underlies retransmission timeout calculation.

name: TCP Retransmission Timeout (RTO)
description: Computes the TCP retransmission timeout as the smoothed RTT plus four times the RTT variation, following Jacobson's algorithm. The variation term adds a safety margin so normal RTT fluctuations do not trigger false retransmissions.
notes: Smoothed RTT and RTT variation are in the same time units. Real implementations also clamp the RTO to a minimum, typically one second, and apply backoff on repeated timeouts.

name: System Availability (MTBF/MTTR)
description: Computes steady-state availability as the mean time between failures divided by the sum of MTBF and the mean time to repair. The result is the fraction of time the system is operational, approaching 1 when repairs are fast relative to failures.
notes: MTBF and MTTR must share the same time unit; the result is dimensionless. This assumes a simple repairable single component and steady-state operation.

name: Annual Downtime (Minutes)
description: Converts an availability figure into the expected downtime per year in minutes, multiplying one minus availability by 525600, the number of minutes in a year. For example, five nines availability leaves about 5.26 minutes.
notes: Availability is a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percentage. The constant 525600 assumes a 365-day year and does not adjust for leap years.

name: dBm to Milliwatts
description: Converts a power level in dBm to milliwatts, raising 10 to the power of the dBm value divided by 10. It undoes the logarithmic decibel scale so, for instance, 30 dBm equals 1000 mW, or 1 watt.
notes: The input is referenced to 1 mW, so 0 dBm equals 1 mW. Negative dBm values give sub-milliwatt powers, and the result is always positive.

name: Free-Space Path Loss
description: Computes free-space path loss in decibels for a radio link from distance and frequency, using 20 log of each plus the constant −147.55 for SI units. Loss increases by 6 dB whenever distance or frequency doubles.
notes: Distance is in meters and frequency in hertz for the −147.55 constant to apply. This is ideal free-space loss only and excludes antenna gains, obstacles, and atmospheric effects.

name: Link Budget (Received Power)
description: Computes the received power in a radio link budget by adding transmit power and both antenna gains, then subtracting the total path loss, all in decibels. It shows the signal level reaching the receiver.
notes: All terms are in decibel units so they add and subtract directly; transmit power in dBm gives received power in dBm. Compare the result to the receiver sensitivity to judge whether the link closes.

name: Expected Bit Errors
description: Computes the expected number of bit errors as the bit error rate times the number of bits transferred. It estimates on average how many bits are corrupted over a given amount of transmitted data.
notes: The bit error rate is a fraction, so a BER of 10⁻⁶ means one error per million bits on average. This is an expected value; actual errors vary and typically follow a Poisson distribution.

name: IPv6 Subnets from Prefix Delta
description: Computes how many IPv6 subnets a site can carve out, equal to 2 raised to the difference between the site prefix and the allocation prefix. Each extra bit of prefix length doubles the number of available subnets.
notes: The site prefix must be numerically larger than the allocation prefix for a positive count. With a /48 allocation and /64 subnets this yields 65536 subnets.

name: One-Way Latency Budget
description: Sums the components of one-way network latency: propagation delay from distance over speed, serialization delay from packet size over link rate, and a fixed processing delay. The total is the time for a packet to travel end to end.
notes: Packet size is in bits and rate in bits per second; distance and speed give propagation. This omits queuing delay, which can dominate under congestion, so it is a best-case estimate.

name: Ring All-Reduce Bytes Sent per GPU
description: Gives the data each GPU sends in a ring all-reduce of a buffer: 2(p − 1)/p times its size, almost independent of the GPU count.
notes: The basis of data-parallel gradient synchronisation (NCCL).

name: Ring All-Reduce Time
description: Estimates all-reduce time with the α–β model: 2(p − 1) steps, each paying latency plus a 1/p slice of the data over the link.
notes: For large buffers the bandwidth term dominates.

name: Pipeline Parallelism Bubble Fraction
description: Gives the share of time GPUs sit idle in a GPipe-style pipeline while it fills and drains (Huang et al. 2019).
notes: Use many more micro-batches than stages to keep the bubble small.

name: ZeRO Memory per GPU (Mixed-Precision Adam)
description: Gives model-state memory per GPU when ZeRO shards optimiser states (stage 1), plus gradients (2), plus parameters (3) (Rajbhandari et al. 2020).
notes: A 7.5 B model needs 120 GB unsharded, 1.875 GB with stage 3 on 64 GPUs; activations come on top.

name: Transformer Activation Memory per Layer
expression: sl * bs * hd * (34 + 5 * na * sl / hd) * bb / 2
description: Estimates the activations stored for backpropagation in one transformer layer, s·b·h·(34 + 5as/h) bytes at 16-bit (Korthikanti et al. 2022).
notes: The 5as/h term is the attention matrix; FlashAttention removes it.

name: Activation Checkpointing Memory (√n Segments)
description: Gives the layer-activations held in memory when storing only k checkpoints and recomputing the rest: n/k + k, minimised at k = √n (Chen et al. 2016).
notes: Costs about one extra forward pass of compute.

name: Largest Finite Value of a Floating-Point Format
description: Gives the largest finite number of an IEEE-style binary format: FP16 (5, 10) 65504, BF16 (8, 7) about 3.39 × 10³⁸.
notes: FP8 E4M3 deviates from IEEE and reaches 448.

name: Machine Epsilon of a Floating-Point Format
description: Gives the gap between 1 and the next representable number: FP32 2⁻²³, FP16 2⁻¹⁰, BF16 2⁻⁷ = 0.0078125.
notes: BF16 keeps FP32's range but only about 2–3 significant digits.

name: Smallest Positive Normal Value of a Floating-Point Format
description: Gives the smallest normal number; gradients below it underflow to subnormals or zero, the reason for loss scaling in FP16.

name: Peak Tensor Throughput of an Accelerator
description: Gives peak dense throughput as units × multiply–adds per clock × clock × 2 FLOPs per multiply–add.
notes: Real training rarely exceeds 40–60 % of this.

name: Performance per Watt
description: Compares accelerators by useful work per unit of power.
notes: Use the same number format and sparsity setting for every chip.

name: Ridge Point of the Roofline
description: Gives the arithmetic intensity at which a kernel stops being memory-bound and becomes compute-bound.
notes: On an H100 a kernel needs about 295 FLOPs per byte to hit peak.

name: Data Transfer Time over a Link
description: Estimates how long it takes to move a model or batch over PCIe, NVLink or a network at a given efficiency.
notes: PCIe 5.0 ×16 is about 64 GB/s each way.

name: GPUs Needed to Hold a Model

variables.label: Overhead for KV cache and activations

description: Gives the minimum GPUs whose combined memory fits the weights plus a margin for cache and activations.
notes: A 70 B model at 16-bit with a 20 % margin needs 168 GB, so three 80 GB GPUs.

name: Serving Cost per Million Tokens
description: Converts an hourly GPU price and throughput into a cost per million generated tokens.
notes: Batching raises throughput and is the main lever on cost.

name: GPUs Needed for a Request Rate
description: Sizes an inference fleet from the request rate, tokens per request, GPU throughput and a headroom target.
notes: Leave headroom for traffic spikes and latency limits.

name: Training Run Carbon Emissions
description: Estimates emissions as GPU energy × facility overhead (PUE) × grid carbon intensity.
notes: Location and time of day change carbon intensity several-fold.

name: Checkpoint Size
description: Gives the storage for a full training checkpoint: weights plus optimiser state (Adam keeps two FP32 moments = 8 bytes).
notes: Weights-only checkpoints for inference are much smaller.

name: Optimal Checkpoint Interval (Young–Daly)

variables.label: Mean time between failures of the job

description: Gives the checkpoint interval that minimises lost work plus checkpoint overhead (Young 1974, Daly 2006).
notes: Large clusters fail often, so the job MTBF shrinks as GPUs are added.

name: Cluster Mean Time Between Failures
description: Gives how often some node in a cluster fails, assuming independent failures: the single-node MTBF divided by the number of nodes.
notes: 2000 nodes at 50,000 h each fail about every 25 hours.

name: Scaling Efficiency
description: Compares multi-GPU throughput with perfect linear scaling from one GPU.
notes: 90 % here; communication and stragglers eat the rest.

name: Gustafson Scaled Speed-up
description: Gives the speed-up when the problem grows with the machine, N − s(N − 1) (Gustafson 1988), the optimistic counterpart of Amdahl's law.
notes: Explains why bigger models keep scaling on bigger clusters.

name: Continuous Batching Throughput Gain
description: Estimates the throughput gain of continuous (in-flight) batching over static batching, where every slot waits for the longest request.
notes: Static batches waste 1 − mean/max of the decode slots.

name: Tokens per Second from Inter-Token Latency
description: Converts the time between generated tokens into the streaming speed a user sees.
notes: Reading speed is roughly 5–8 tokens per second.

name: Prompt Cache Cost Saving

variables.label: Share of input tokens served from cache
Cached price as a share of normal

description: Gives the fraction of input-token cost saved by prompt caching.
notes: Keep stable content at the start of the prompt to maximise hits.

name: Data Loader Throughput Needed
description: Gives the input bandwidth the storage and data pipeline must sustain so accelerators never wait for data.
notes: Image and video training is often limited here, not by compute.

name: Tensor Parallel All-Reduce Volume per Layer
description: Gives the activations all-reduced per transformer layer in Megatron-style tensor parallelism: two in the forward pass and two in the backward pass, each of size b·s·h.
notes: Because of this volume, tensor parallelism is kept inside one NVLink node.

name: Expert Capacity (Mixture of Experts)
description: Gives how many tokens each expert can accept per batch; overflow tokens are dropped or rerouted (Switch Transformer).
notes: Capacity factors of 1.0–1.25 are common in training.

name: Memory Bandwidth Utilisation
description: Gives the share of peak memory bandwidth a kernel actually achieved, the key efficiency figure for decoding.
notes: Well-tuned decode kernels reach 70–90 %.

name: Batch Size at Compute-Bound Decoding
description: Estimates the decode batch size at which reading the weights stops being the bottleneck: each weight byte read serves 2/bytes FLOPs per sequence.
notes: Around 295 on an H100 at 16-bit; below it, extra batch is almost free.

name: Weight Streaming Time for One Forward Pass
description: Gives the time just to read all weights from memory once, the floor on per-step decode latency at small batch.
notes: Quantising to 4 bits cuts it by 4× versus 16-bit.

name: Quantised Model Size
description: Gives weight storage for a given average bits per weight; group-wise formats add about 0.5 bit for scales.
notes: 70 B at 4.5 bits is about 39 GB.

name: Energy per Generated Token
description: Gives the energy spent per output token from power draw and throughput.
notes: Multiply by 1000 tokens and divide by 3600 for Wh per thousand tokens.

name: Little's Law for Concurrent Requests
description: Gives the average number of requests in flight, L = λW, which sets the batch the server must hold (Little 1961).
notes: Holds for any stable queue regardless of distribution.

name: Tail Latency at Fan-Out

variables.label: Chance one backend call is slow

description: Gives the chance that a request waiting on n parallel calls hits at least one slow call (Dean and Barroso 2013, "The Tail at Scale").
notes: With 100 calls, a 1-in-100 slowdown affects 63 % of requests.

name: Cluster Bisection Bandwidth (Fat Tree)
description: Gives the bandwidth across the middle of a fat-tree network: half the hosts talking to the other half at full rate, reduced by oversubscription.
notes: AI training fabrics are usually built non-oversubscribed (1:1).

name: Fat-Tree Hosts for k-Port Switches
description: Gives the hosts a three-tier fat tree of identical k-port switches can connect at full bisection bandwidth (Al-Fares et al. 2008).
notes: 64-port switches support 65,536 hosts.
